adds.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
adds.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

adds.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

records.note: Japan's documented placement practice is by registered sex: trans inmates are held in the men's or women's facility matching their family-register sex, not their gender identity. A trans man registered female was held at Gifu's Kasamatsu women's prison, where a bar-association 'warning' (Sep 2023) pressed for male treatment accommodation, and trans activist Tomoya Asanuma, detained in 2024, was held among men in pre-trial detention with initially denied hormones and hostile conditions (HRW, Jun 2025). No statutory rule requiring placement by gender identity was found; accommodation disputes are handled through bar-association pressure and case-by-case practices.

adds.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
adds.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

adds.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
adds.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

records.note: Thailand's Corrections Department separates transgender inmates from cisgender men nationwide (a policy the department dates to 1993), so trans prisoners like Theerayut Charoenpakdee (2017) are held in dedicated LGBTQ blocks (e.g. Pattaya Remand Prison) rather than regular men's wings (NBC/AP, Jan 2017). Formally, placement tracks legal sex: activist Nachacha Kongudom was put in a men's prison in June 2015 because Thai law still classed her as male (Coconuts, Aug 2016). In 2016 the department launched the Min Buri LGBT-facility pilot to curb abuse of trans inmates, which activists supported only on condition that it be optional, not obligatory.
